checkpoints: Names the guarantee precisely as exactly-once delivery — the provider is invoked exactly once per messageId.
Explicitly flags that this is NOT exactly-once at every layer / not an absolute end-to-end guarantee.
Half 1 — the queue itself is at-least-once: a crash before ack means the job gets redelivered, so nothing is silently lost.
Half 2 — SET NX dedup never re-sends: whoever atomically claims dedup:{messageId} is the one that sends; every other claimant no-ops.
Residual seam: if the dedup key gets claimed and then the provider dies before actually sending, a later retry is deduped even though nothing ever arrived.
Residual seam: if the dedup TTL expires before a very late retry shows up, the message gets sent again (duplicate).
Explains why true end-to-end exactly-once isn't done: it would need a real two-phase commit with the provider, which is too costly in practice.
States the practical fallback: settle for at-least-once + an idempotent consumer, and for critical messages persist "sent" durably instead of trusting the TTL alone.
Atomicity and correct time are two different guarantees, and only one of them is fixed here.
Running read-refill-decrement-write as one Lua script guarantees no other command can interleave mid-script, closing the concurrency race between two requests hitting the same key at once.
It says nothing about whether the now value each caller passes in is itself trustworthy.

elapsed = now - lastRefill is computed from whatever the calling producer's own Date.now() returned, so if two producer hosts have clocks skewed relative to each other, one instance's script call computes a different number of elapsed refill windows than another's would for the exact same real-world moment.
This causes over-refilling (letting through more traffic than the limit intends) or under-refilling (rejecting traffic that should have been allowed), depending on which way the skew points.
The fix has nothing to do with adding more atomicity — the script is already atomic.

The actual fix is to stop trusting each caller's local clock and instead read now from Redis's own clock inside the script itself (redis.call("TIME")), so every producer computes elapsed against exactly the same single time source.

General lesson: an atomic operation is only as correct as the inputs fed into it — a hidden input still sourced independently by N different callers (each producer's wall clock) can undermine correctness just as thoroughly as a non-atomic race would.

When a producer packs every requested channel into the data of a single queue job, the broker only has one pass/fail outcome to react to — it cannot tell that push already succeeded and only email needs another try.

A for-loop that awaits push, then email, then sms inside one processor function has no isolation between channels: an exception thrown while sending email propagates out of the processor and is treated as a failure of the entire job, not just the email step.

Because the retry unit in a job queue is the job itself, retrying that failed job re-runs the processor from the top — so push, which already sent successfully, fires again and reaches the user as a duplicate notification.

The mismatch driving this bug is that the desired unit of retry is one channel, while the actual unit of retry the queue provides is one job; bundling multiple channels into a single job collapses that distinction.

The structural fix is fan-out at the producer: instead of enqueuing one job whose data holds an array of channels, enqueue one separate job per channel (for example via a bulk-add call), using the channel as the job name and giving each job only that channel's payload.
With one job per channel, a failure in the email job causes the broker to retry only that job; the push and sms jobs already completed independently and are left untouched, so they cannot be re-sent.

Wrapping each provider call in a try/catch that swallows the error is not a valid fix, because it prevents the failure from ever surfacing to the queue — the email job is never marked failed, so it is never retried, and the notification is silently lost instead of duplicated.

A meaningful way to verify the fix is to enqueue a multi-channel request where the email provider fails on its first attempt, then confirm push and sms were each delivered exactly once while only the email job shows a retry that eventually succeeds.

Keeping a rate limiter's remaining-token count on a private field of a service instance means every replica running behind a load balancer holds its own independent copy of that count, so the aggregate throughput allowed across all replicas is roughly N times the intended per-key limit.

In-memory counter state does not survive a process restart: a redeploy or crash-restart re-initializes the field to its starting capacity, silently resetting the limiter to full even though no time-based refill was actually earned.

Implementing a Redis-backed limiter as a plain `GET` followed by a plain `SET` is not atomic — the two calls are separate network round trips, so two concurrent requests can both read the same stored token count, both compute the same decremented value, and both write it back, losing one decrement and letting more requests through than the limit allows (a TOCTOU race).

The fix is to collapse the entire read-refill-decrement-write sequence into a single Lua script executed via Redis `EVAL`, because Redis runs each Lua script to completion on its single command thread, so no other client's command can interleave in the middle of the sequence.

The bucket must be keyed per logical entity being limited (for example `user:channel`) so that every replica reads and writes the same shared counter in Redis instead of each maintaining its own state, and the key should carry a TTL/expiry so an idle bucket is cleaned up automatically instead of accumulating in Redis forever.

Overshooting a provider's send-rate limit is a production-severity blocker rather than a style nitpick, because the sending IP or account can get throttled or blocked by the notification provider/carrier, taking down message delivery for the whole system.

This class of bug passes cleanly in a single-instance local or test environment because there is only one process and no real concurrent network round trip to expose the race — it only manifests once the service is actually scaled out to multiple replicas under concurrent load.

Verifying the fix requires a concurrency test: fire capacity-plus-one requests at the same key simultaneously (ideally from at least two separate instances or connections) and assert that exactly one request is rejected, which proves the counting is atomic and shared rather than racy or per-process.

A catch block that simply rethrows an error so the queue's built-in attempts and exponential backoff retry the job is not the same as failover: it re-invokes the exact same primary provider after each backoff delay, so if the primary is genuinely down, every retry hits the same dead endpoint again and the recipient waits through several seconds of dead time for nothing.

Genuine failover switches to a fallback provider within the same attempt — catching the primary's failure and immediately calling the fallback before the job handler returns — rather than letting the error escape to the queue and waiting on a scheduled retry; only when both the primary and the fallback fail should the error propagate to the broker for an actual job-level retry.

On an at-least-once queue, a message can be redelivered because a worker crashes right before the implicit acknowledgment, or because an earlier attempt is retried, and a processor with no idempotency check will send that message again — for a login OTP email that is a user-facing double-send bug, not a cosmetic detail.

Deduplication needs a stable message identifier, supplied by the caller or generated once at the producer, namespaced per delivery channel (for example combining a base message id with the channel name), so the same logical send across retries or channels can be recognized as one intent to deliver rather than several.

Before dispatching, the processor should atomically acquire the message id as a key in a shared store — such as a Redis SET with NX and an expiry — and proceed with sending only if that acquisition succeeds; if the key already exists, the send is skipped because delivery has already happened or is already in flight.

A senior-level PR review separates true blockers — a delivery path that can silently double-send, and a fallback provider that is wired into the constructor but never actually invoked — from nitpicks, and asks about the author's intent, such as whether retrying only the primary was a deliberate interim choice or simply unfinished work, instead of just declaring the code wrong.

Verifying the fix requires two specific tests: one that forces the primary provider to fail and asserts the fallback delivers the message within the same attempt with no multi-second wait, and one that redelivers the same message id twice and asserts the underlying provider's send is invoked exactly once.
The core problem is decoupling the high-throughput ingest path from the processing path, not the COUNT(*) query itself
Synchronous writes that block the response on an INSERT completing cannot sustain tens of thousands of events per second
That synchronous design pushes backpressure onto clients: they wait longer, time out, or get rejected once the DB saturates
An append-only log like Kafka lets the producer append the event and return immediately (fire-and-forget, HTTP 202) without waiting for the consumer to process it
The consumer reads the log at its own pace, independent of how fast the producer writes
During a traffic spike the log buffers the burst so the consumer can lag and later catch up without losing events, instead of pushing backpressure onto the client or DB
Ingest and processing are decoupled in both speed (producer never waits on consumer) and time (consumer can process later than the event was written)
Event time is when the click actually happened, stamped by the producer into eventTime at message creation
Processing time is when the consumer handles the record — a distinct time axis from event time
Because messages travel across networks with unavoidable, uneven delay, events can arrive late and out of the order they actually happened in

Windowing by processing time assigns a click to whichever minute the consumer is in when it receives the message, not the minute it actually happened (e.g. a 10:00 click arriving at 10:02 lands in the 10:02 window)
When the consumer lags and then suddenly catches up on a backlog, all those delayed clicks get dumped into whatever window is current at that moment, spiking it
That same catch-up leaves the windows the clicks truly belong to undercounted, so the chart is wrong and unstable — driven by the pipeline's own processing speed rather than real user behavior

Windowing by eventTime instead keeps every click in the minute window it truly happened regardless of consumer speed, at the cost of needing a watermark mechanism to decide how late an event can still be admitted

A counter that accumulates a lifetime total per IP and never resets measures everything that IP has ever done, not how fast it is clicking right now — fraud detection needs a rate, not a cumulative total.

A shared office NAT or a genuinely popular ad's IP can rack up ordinary traffic over days and eventually cross a fixed lifetime threshold, producing a false positive on completely legitimate traffic with zero relation to any burst.

A lifetime counter has no concept of a burst: an IP that has been quiet for weeks and suddenly fires hundreds of clicks in seconds gets flagged no faster than one that trickles in slowly, because both are just adding to the same never-resetting number.
An ever-growing Map keyed by IP that is never cleared is also an unbounded memory leak, and once an IP is flagged it stays flagged forever with no way to cool down.

Keying counts by (IP, windowStart) instead of IP alone — for example a tumbling one-minute window compared against a per-window threshold — turns the signal into clicks-per-window rather than clicks-ever, catching a real spike the moment it happens and resetting cleanly every window.

Because the underlying signal is IP alone with a fixed constant threshold, a botnet can trivially evade it by rotating through many IPs, keeping each individual IP's count comfortably under threshold while the aggregate attack volume stays huge.

A strict tumbling window has its own boundary gap: a burst split across two adjacent windows can stay under threshold in each window even though it is really one continuous spike, so a sliding or hopping window is needed to close that gap.

A robust redesign layers signals beyond IP — device fingerprint, user agent, click-pattern behavior — and derives thresholds adaptively from each IP's own recent baseline instead of applying one hard constant to every IP on the platform.

The redesign can be validated with targeted tests: a burst of clicks from one IP within a single window must flag, the same total volume spread evenly over weeks must not flag, and a burst split across a window boundary should expose the tumbling-window gap.

A `Set<string>` that records every clickId ever seen and is never evicted grows monotonically with total traffic, so under billions of clicks per day the process eventually exhausts memory and OOMs — this is a data-structure-shape problem, not a leak in the counting logic itself.

Because that same `seen` set lives only in process memory, any restart (deploy, crash, rebalance) wipes it clean, so a clickId that Kafka redelivers after the restart looks brand-new to the consumer and gets counted a second time, silently inflating ad-click totals.

These are two independent failures with two independent root causes — unbounded growth causes the OOM, loss of in-memory state on restart causes the recount — and conflating them into one fix (e.g. just periodically clearing the set) solves neither properly.

Bounding memory only requires catching duplicates that arrive within the realistic redelivery/retry window, not remembering a clickId forever, so scoping dedup to a TTL turns an ever-growing set into a structure whose size is capped by window length times throughput.

`SET clickId 1 NX EX <ttlSeconds>` in Redis makes the has-it-been-seen check and the mark-it-as-seen write a single atomic round-trip, which is what `NX` buys over a plain get-then-set; a compacted RocksDB column family is the local alternative when a network hop per event is too costly.

Moving the dedup index into an external, durable store (Redis or a replicated/persisted RocksDB) makes it survive process restarts, since a redelivered clickId is still found and correctly rejected instead of looking new — this is what actually fixes the recount bug, separately from the TTL fix for memory.

Kafka transactional producers with `read_committed` consumers give true exactly-once delivery and would eliminate the dedup problem entirely, but that comes at real throughput and operational-complexity cost compared to a TTL-based external store.

A TTL-based fix trades one failure mode for a narrower one: a duplicate that arrives after the window has expired is no longer recognized and gets re-counted, so the window must be sized to the slowest realistic retry rather than the median, and an external store adds a network round-trip to every `record()` call — so validating the fix means confirming memory stays flat over hours, a post-restart redelivery is still rejected, and p99 latency hasn't just moved the cost from memory into the network hop.

Calling `this.ch.insert(...)` once per incoming Kafka message instead of accumulating counts and flushing on an interval is the write-side mistake: every insert call creates a new part on disk regardless of row count, so firing one insert per click under real traffic produces thousands of tiny parts per second that the background merge scheduler cannot keep up with.

ClickHouse's `ReplacingMergeTree` (and MergeTree-family engines generally) is designed around large, infrequent batched inserts, not high-frequency single-row inserts — the fix is to go back to bucketing counts in memory (as the original aggregator's record/flush split did) and calling `insert` once every few seconds with the whole accumulated batch, leaving the total row count unchanged but drastically reducing the number of INSERT calls.

Running `SELECT ... FROM ad_click_counts FINAL` on every dashboard load is the separate read-side mistake: `FINAL` forces ClickHouse to merge all parts for the matching keys at query time rather than relying on background merges, so the more unmerged parts accumulate (worsened by the write-path bug), the more work every concurrent dashboard viewer's query does.

The read-path fix is to swap the hot dashboard query to `argMax(count, insertedAt)` — which requires adding a version/timestamp column to disambiguate rows sharing the same `(adId, windowStart)` key — and to reserve `FINAL` only for rare, non-hot-path queries where exact freshness matters more than latency.

A single ad going viral concentrates all its clicks within one window onto a single `(adId, windowStart)` key, creating a hotspot for both flush contention and `argMax` grouping even after the batching fix is applied.

Hashing an extra sub-key such as `adId|bucket_n` (chosen for example by hashing `clickId`) spreads writes for a hot key across multiple rows, and summing across those sub-buckets on read collapses them back into the correct per-ad total without changing the reported numbers.

Batching trades away some freshness: ClickHouse's view of the data lags behind by up to the flush interval, and any unflushed buckets are lost if the aggregator crashes before the next flush — an acceptable trade-off for a near-real-time reporting dashboard but not for anything requiring exact real-time counts.

A fix should not be considered done just because the diff looks correct — it needs to be validated by re-running the same load profile before and after and confirming that ClickHouse CPU, active part count, and dashboard p99 latency all return to baseline while the reported numbers per `(adId, windowStart)` stay unchanged.
